title: Articles 33–35 — Armed forces, martial law, and Part III legislation

content.overview: Article 33 empowers Parliament to determine by law to what extent any of the Part III rights shall apply to members of the Armed Forces, members of forces charged with maintenance of public order, persons employed in intelligence or telecommunication for those forces, and persons employed in or connected with the telecommunication system of those forces. Article 34 restricts Part III rights while martial law is in force in any area, and allows Parliament to indemnify persons for acts done in connection with its maintenance. Article 35 gives Parliament power to legislate on specified Part III matters, including punishment for acts declared offences in Part III, and bars State legislatures from making laws on those matters except as Article 35 provides.
content.study: Article 33 is a parliamentary modification power, not a blanket repeal of Part III for soldiers. Article 34 is martial law, not an ordinary emergency. Article 35 is competence, not a right.

sections.heading: Article 33
sections.body: Parliament may determine extent of Part III application to Armed Forces and related forces.

learningObjectives: State Article 35 as a legislative allocation.
enhancement.definition: Articles 33 to 35 let Parliament modify Part III for specified forces, restrict rights under martial law, and exclusively legislate on listed Part III matters.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Modification must be by Parliament's law under Article 33. A force standing order is not itself that law. Martial law is not the same as a constitutional emergency.
essentialIngredients: Martial law actually in force for Article 34
Article 35 matter identified before a State law is pleaded
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Article 33 lists four classes: armed forces, public-order forces, intelligence or telecommunication employees for those forces, and related telecommunication personnel. Parliament may restrict or abrogate Part III rights so as to ensure proper discharge of duties and maintenance of discipline. Article 34 applies only while martial law is in force in an area and validates indemnity legislation notwithstanding Part III. Article 35(a) gives Parliament power, and State legislatures no power, to make laws on prescribed residence under Article 16(3), empowering courts under Article 32(3), punishment for Part III offences, and Parliament's laws under Articles 33 and 34. Article 35(b) continues existing eligible laws until altered or repealed by Parliament.
examples: A disciplinary statute made by Parliament restricts assembly rights of armed-force members. Article 33 is the source to read.
A State Act tries to punish an Article 17 offence. Article 35 allocates that punishment law to Parliament.
An ordinary curfew order is called martial law. Article 34 requires martial law in force in the area.
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify the class of person and the law-making body. Apply Article 33 only to a parliamentary law. Do not treat Article 35 as a fundamental right.
distinctions: Article 33 parliamentary law vs a force order
Article 34 martial law vs a constitutional emergency
Article 35 competence vs a Part III right
Armed forces vs all public servants

keyTakeaways: Article 33 is Parliament's power, for listed forces.
It is to ensure duty and discipline.
Article 34 is martial law and indemnity.
Article 35 gives Parliament listed Part III laws.
State legislatures are excluded from those matters.
